objects.svg: Six photographs in two rows: frog, eagle and elephant above tiger, penguin and gorilla. Their relationships can depend on appearance, biological category or other properties. The grid is a layout only; position does not encode similarity.
stimulus_028.png: A photograph of a tiger standing on wet rocks at the edge of a pool, facing the camera. The animal is the referent, the photograph is one depiction of it, and the pixel array is a numerical encoding of the photograph.
appearance.svg: Left: the original tiger photograph. Middle: the same photograph with its pixel intensities multiplied by one half, making it darker. Right: a gorilla photograph. The first change alters the image values and keeps the object; the second changes the depicted object.
pixel_vector.svg: The tiger photograph as 224 by 224 single-channel values, reduced to 28 by 28 pixels. The 784 values are listed in row order to form a vector, wrapped into seven bands for display; the interactive version shows selected entries as code.
neural_response.svg: Left: a coronal MRI from Bao et al. (2020), Figure 4c, showing functionally localized IT patches in monkey M3, and a cropped detail from Extended Data Figure 8a marking three example recording sites in the Stubby2 patch, with a 5 mm scale bar. The two views are separate and do not show the locations of all 482 neurons. Right: the monochrome cat stimulus in a light frame, above a bar plot of firing rates for all 482 units. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 100; the largest value is about 80.75. There are 479 available values; small marks below the axis flag missing measurements at positions 429, 430 and 457, which are not zeros. Bao recorded every well-isolated neuron encountered at the targeted sites, with no selectivity screen. The experiment used 1,224 rendered views, each shown for 250 ms and repeated 4–8 times; activity was counted 60–220 ms after onset.
network_stages.svg: A sequence connects image, early layers, later layers and class scores. Each layer computes a new pattern from the preceding one. Residual connections and other architecture-specific operations are omitted.
matched_network.svg: The Bao stimulus shown with the IT recording, beside a bar chart of its first 32 stored late ResNet-18 activations from an ImageNet-trained model. The full vector has 4,096 entries sampled from the flattened spatial activations, not 4,096 channels.
bold_response.svg: A BOLD5000 photograph of a dog beside two bar charts for participant CSI1: early visual cortex on the left, lateral occipital complex on the right. Each chart shows the first 16 voxels in stored order, out of 210 and 152 voxels. Values fall above or below the voxel's baseline. Each value is the average of the third and fourth scans after stimulus onset; these are blood-oxygenation responses, not firing rates.
features_point.svg: Six images plotted by mean intensity and RMS contrast. The tiger is highlighted at approximately (72.7, 40.6), with dashed guides to its two components.
features_vector.svg: The same axes and image positions as the previous figure. A blue vector runs from the origin to the tiger at approximately (72.7, 40.6), labelled with bold x; the axis labels are the italic scalar components.
more_coordinates.svg: Three columns show the same BOLD5000 response with the first two voxels, the first three, and all 210 early visual voxels. The initial entries stay the same as the list grows. In the last column, a vertical ellipsis stands for the middle entries and the final value shown is component 210. Adding a dimension adds a component to the list.
response_matrix.svg: Rows are six animal photographs; columns are the first 12 stored network activations. Each colored cell is the activation of one entry for one image, and a row is that image's response vector. The six by 4,096 matrix is shown in part; color encodes activation, not similarity.
peterson2018_fig3a_animals_mds.png: Three published nonmetric multidimensional-scaling maps of the same animal images, from human judgments, raw network representations, and a learned transformation of the network features. Each map places images so that their separations approximate the corresponding dissimilarities. The arrangement of the animals changes from map to map. The axes are display coordinates, and orientation is arbitrary.
scaling.svg: The vector x=(3,1) runs from the origin to (3,1). Multiplying by two gives 2x=(6,2), in the same direction at twice the length; both components are multiplied by the scalar.
addition.svg: Vectors x=(3,1) and y=(1,3) start at the origin. Moving y so that its tail sits at the tip of x gives the sum (4,4), with y's length and direction unchanged. Dashed guides complete the parallelogram. The mean, (x+y)/2=(2,2), lies halfway from the origin to the sum.
size_words.svg: Photographs of a frog, tiger, gorilla and elephant illustrate the animal words. The semantic-projection model receives word vectors, not these photographs, and asks whether a direction through word-vector space recovers judgments of animal size.
difference.svg: The displacement from x=(3,1) to y=(1,3) is y−x=(−2,2): two units left and two units up. It is drawn from the tip of x to the tip of y, whereas a position vector starts at the origin.
dot_product.svg: Vectors x=(3,1) and w=(1,1) begin at the origin; phi marks the angle between them. Their dot product is 3×1+1×1=4, which also equals the product of their lengths times the cosine of phi. Here w has length square root of two.
projection.svg: Vector x=(3,1) is projected onto the unit vector w=(1,1)/√2, whose line is extended by a dashed guide. The perpendicular from the tip of x meets that line at p=(2,2), marked with a right angle. The scalar projection is wᵀx=2√2 and the projected vector is p=(wᵀx)w. The residual x−p=(1,−1) is orthogonal to w.
semantic-projection.png: A published schematic places animal-word vectors in an embedding space and projects them onto a direction running from small to large. Perpendicular drops turn each vector into a position along that direction, and these scores are compared with human size judgments. The paper defines each direction by combining several anchor word pairs.
structured_pixels.svg: The reduced tiger image beside an array of independently sampled random grayscale values. Both are points in the same 784-dimensional pixel space; natural images occupy a small part of it.
euclidean.svg: Object A is at (3,1) and object B at (1,3). They differ by two units along each axis. Dashed legs form a right triangle whose hypotenuse, the distance between A and B, is √(2²+2²)=√8.
distance_ranking.svg: Three response patterns: A=(1,1), B=(4,4) and C=(1,−1). A and B have the same direction but different lengths; C is perpendicular to A. Euclidean distance ranks C closer to A: d(A,C)=2 versus d(A,B)=√18. Cosine dissimilarity ranks B closer: dcos(A,B)=0 versus dcos(A,C)=1.
relu.svg: The rectified linear unit outputs zero for negative inputs and returns the input unchanged for positive inputs. A unit that is inactive for every image in a set gives an all-zero column in the response matrix.
dead_column.svg: Two image rows, (1,0,0) and (0,1,0); the third unit is zero for both. Without that column each row's mean is one half and the correlation is −1. With it each row's mean is one third and the correlation is −0.5. Euclidean distance and cosine similarity are unchanged.
animal_rdm.svg: A square matrix of Euclidean distances between every pair of the six animal images, computed on all 4,096 stored late ResNet-18 activations. Rows and columns share the same order. The diagonal is zero and the matrix is symmetric. The table below lists every distance.
triangle_bound.svg: A path runs from A to B by a segment of length one, then from B to C by another segment of length one. The endpoints can be at most two apart, reached when the path is straight; bending the path brings them closer. This is the triangle inequality.
cosine_triangle.svg: Three unit vectors at 0, 45 and 90 degrees. The cosine dissimilarity between the outer two is one. Each adjacent pair has dissimilarity 1−1/√2, approximately 0.293, and the two sum to approximately 0.586, less than one. Cosine dissimilarity therefore violates the triangle inequality.
11_same_score.svg: Point arrangements for models with equal task accuracy: the same performance score can come with different internal response geometries.
basis.svg: The vector (3,2) in the standard basis is re-expressed in a rotated orthonormal basis with e₁=(1,1)/√2 and e₂=(−1,1)/√2. Its new coordinates are 5/√2 and −1/√2, approximately 3.536 and −0.707. Recombining them with the rotated basis vectors gives back (3,2). The vector and its length stay fixed; its coordinates depend on the basis.
codes.svg: Three matrices of six stimuli by eight units contrast coding schemes. Localist: each stimulus activates one distinct unit. Dense distributed: each stimulus uses all units with varying strengths. Sparse distributed: each stimulus activates two units.
network_maps.svg: The Bao cat image, converted to RGB and center-cropped to 224 by 224, and channels 1 and 2 at the early, middle and late ResNet-18 stages. Their spatial grids are 56 by 56, 14 by 14 and 7 by 7; the full stages contain 64, 256 and 512 channels. Light color is zero, and color intensity rises to the maximum for that image and stage; scales can differ between stages. The live explorer adds layer2, six images, all channels and a table of the selected map. A unit is one channel at one spatial position.
spike_to_rate.svg: A schematic: a tungsten electrode beside a neuron picks up extracellular spikes. Seven spikes fall in a 160 millisecond window, from 60 to 220 milliseconds after image onset. Seven spikes divided by 0.16 seconds gives 43.75 spikes per second (43.75 Hz), the window Bao et al. used to count responses.
pixel_bars.svg: Left: the tiger photograph from the pixel explorer. Middle: its 28 by 28 grayscale version. Right: all 784 grayscale values as bars, read left to right across each row and then down to the next row. Each bar is one pixel, and its height is the intensity on a 0–255 scale. The horizontal axis is pixel position, not time. The layout matches the later cat neural-response figure, where each bar is a neuron.
network_vector.svg: The Bao cat image passed through an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18. In the late layer, channel 376 is a 7 by 7 map; read row by row it gives 49 activations, the first four 0.00, 1.80, 2.41 and 2.36. Concatenating all 512 channels in order gives 25,088 values; flattening keeps every value and does not average over space. Assignment 1 uses a fixed sample of 4,096 of these entries. Channel 376 has the largest spatial mean for this image; the interactive explorer shows every channel and all four stages.
bold_surface_vectors.svg: Top: cortical surfaces from Gao et al. (2025), Figure 6b, with early visual cortex in red and the lateral occipital complex (LOC) in green, defined by a localizer scan. The colors mark regions, not responses to the dog. Bottom: the ImageNet dog photograph shown in the experiment, beside the responses of all 210 early visual and 152 LOC voxels of participant CSI1, left hemisphere. Each bar is one voxel in stored order, and each value is the average of the third and fourth scans after onset. Each region gives one ordered response vector.
electrode_to_rate.svg: A tiger photograph enters a simplified macaque visual pathway, drawn after DiCarlo, Zoccolan and Rust (2012), Figure 3A: retina, lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), V1, V2, V4 and inferotemporal cortex (IT). Feedback and parallel routes are omitted. The next panel shows an illustrative extracellular voltage trace with seven spikes from one neuron between 60 and 220 milliseconds. Seven spikes divided by 0.160 seconds gives 43.75 spikes per second (Hz). The interactive version reveals the panels in three steps.
tigers_monkey.svg: Three photographs from the assignment image set, left to right: A, a tiger standing on rocky ground; B, a tiger facing the camera in water; C, a monkey. The two tigers differ in pose, visible body parts and background but share a category; tiger–monkey comparisons cross categories.
magritte-1929-lacma.webp: René Magritte’s 1929 painting The Treachery of Images, at LACMA. A brown smoking pipe on a beige ground above a cursive French inscription, “Ceci n’est pas une pipe” (“This is not a pipe”). The painting separates an object from an image that depicts it. Photograph © Museum Associates/LACMA; artwork © C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.
rgb_channels.svg: The color tiger photograph and its red, green and blue channel images. The 224 by 224 image holds 150,528 channel values. At row 112, column 112 the RGB values are [172, 129, 105], or approximately [0.675, 0.506, 0.412] after division by 255, shown as three bars. In the interactive version any pixel can be selected by pointer, arrow keys or row and column controls.
tungsten-tips-en2023-fig5.jpg: Scanning electron micrographs of two tungsten microelectrode tips from Oikawa et al. (2023), Figure 5, with a 20 micrometer scale bar, on a dark background. These are typical tips, not the electrodes Bao et al. used.
hubel-wiesel-simple-poster.png: Still from the historical Hubel–Wiesel film on a simple cell in cat visual cortex. A projected diagonal light bar crosses the screen while the experimenter marks response locations. In the film, clicks make the neuron's spikes audible, and its activity changes with the bar's position and orientation. The interactive version has a captioned player and a text description.
yamins-dicarlo-2016-framed.svg: Figure 1b–c of Yamins and DiCarlo (2016): ventral-stream areas above a candidate hierarchical convolutional model. A macaque brain inset locates V1, V2, V4 and posterior, central and anterior IT; the upper pathway also includes retinal ganglion cells (RGC) and the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). Arrows connect successive populations, including recurrent and feedback connections. Below, stacked sheets represent the feature maps at successive network layers; small red boxes mark local receptive fields, and a lower-right inset lists filtering, thresholding, pooling and normalization. Green dashed arrows mark proposed correspondences between model stages and brain areas, to be tested with neural data. The network is schematic, and the 100-ms presentation belongs to the source figure; Bao's images were shown for 250 ms.
imagenet-ensemble-history.svg: Selected ImageNet top-5 test accuracies by benchmark year: five AlexNet-family models 83.6% (2012); Clarifai ensemble 88.3% (2013); VGG seven-model submission 92.7% and GoogLeNet seven-model submission 93.3% (2014); six-model ResNet ensemble 96.4% (2015). Top-5 counts a prediction correct when the true category is among the five highest-ranked. The entries are ensembles trained and evaluated in different ways, so the curve does not isolate the effect of depth.
trials_averaging.svg: An illustrative example for one image i: three neurons respond over three repetitions, (2,5,1), (4,3,2) and (3,4,3), in spikes per second over a fixed window. Averaging component by component gives the mean vector x with superscript (i), equal to (3,4,2). The neurons keep their order.
transpose_column_row.svg: The mean response for image i as a 3-by-1 column vector with entries 3, 4, 2. Transposing it gives a 1-by-3 row with 3, 4, 2 in the same order. Bold x denotes the vector, superscript (i) the image, and upright T the transpose. The row can then be stored as row i of a response matrix.
similarity_fallback.svg: Two nonmetric multidimensional-scaling maps of the same 120 animal images from Assignment 1 and Peterson et al.: one from human pairwise ratings, one from the late activations of an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18. Each point is one image. Human dissimilarity is 10 minus the mean 0–10 rating; network dissimilarity is one minus the correlation between activation vectors. The maps are centered and scaled separately and are not aligned to each other; the axes are arbitrary. The explorer highlights the same image in both maps with a larger photograph; the static figure highlights the tiger from the opening.
training_loop.svg: Supervised image classification. A training image passes through a network with adjustable weights to produce predicted class probabilities. Comparing the prediction with the true label gives a classification loss, and a learning algorithm uses the loss to update the weights. Repeating this over many labeled images lowers the average loss and changes the network's internal responses. After training, the weights are fixed while representations are extracted. The probability bars are an example: monkey is shown as more probable than the correct label, tiger.
pixel_scaling.svg: The 28 by 28 tiger array before and after every intensity is multiplied by 0.5; the second image is darker. Beside the images, the first four entries of the 784-entry vector and of its scaled version show every entry halved and the order unchanged. Both images share the same 0–255 display scale; the scaled values keep their fractions.
image_blend.svg: The 28 by 28 tiger and gorilla images on either side of their pixelwise mean. At every location, the middle intensity is half the tiger value plus half the gorilla value. All three share the same 0–255 grayscale scale. The mean overlays the two images; the animal shapes are not morphed. The live version varies the weight from zero (tiger) through one half (the mean) to one (gorilla).
mixup_targets.svg: A mixup training example: the input is a 50–50 pixelwise mixture of the tiger and gorilla images, and its target gives weight 0.5 to the tiger class, 0.5 to the gorilla class and zero to all others. The same mixing weight is used for the image and its target.
difference-0.svg: Two position vectors from the origin: x ends at (3,1) and y at (1,3).
difference-1.svg: The same two vectors, now with an arrow from x=(3,1) to y=(1,3). Its components are y minus x=(−2,2): two units left and two units up. The arrow starts at x, whereas a position vector starts at the origin.
projection-0.svg: Vector x=(3,1) and the unit vector w=(1,1)/square root of two start at the origin. A dashed line extends w.
projection-1.svg: The same vectors, with a dashed perpendicular from x=(3,1) to the line of w, meeting it at (2,2) with a right-angle marker.
projection-2.svg: The same construction, with the projected vector p from the origin to (2,2). Its signed length along w is w transpose x=2 square root of two, and p=(w transpose x)w. The residual x minus p=(1,−1) is perpendicular to w.
animal_distances.svg: The three tiger photographs from the opening slide (A and B near mirror images of one another, B and C in the same walking pose), represented once by their 784 pixel intensities and once by 4,096 late ResNet-18 activations. Each triangle keeps all three Euclidean distances; the two have separate scales and no feature axes. In pixels, B–C (same pose, same grass) is the closest pair; in the network, A–B (the mirror pair) is. The live version slides between the two maps.
image_blend_live.png: The 28 by 28 tiger and gorilla images on either side of their pixelwise mean. At every location, the middle intensity is half the tiger value plus half the gorilla value. All three share the same 0–255 grayscale scale. The mean overlays the two images; the animal shapes are not morphed. The live version varies the weight from zero (tiger) through one half (the mean) to one (gorilla). The first input x is blue, the second input y magenta, and the result green.
dot_product-1.svg: Vectors x=(3,1) and w=(1,1) begin at the origin; phi marks the angle between them. Their dot product is 3×1+1×1=4, which also equals the product of their lengths times the cosine of phi. Here w has length square root of two.
shared_zeros.svg: Late ResNet-18 activation profiles over the same 4,096 stored features for the tiger (blue) and the gorilla (magenta), beside their photographs, on identical scales. Green marks below each baseline flag the 879 entries that are zero for both images. Removing those positions from both vectors leaves 3,217 entries. Correlation dissimilarity changes from 0.8970717146 to 1.0109306350, because each vector is recentered on a different mean; Euclidean distance stays 125.6646924 and cosine dissimilarity 0.6352952988. None of these features is zero across all 120 images.
triangle_constraint.svg: Three image representations, bold x with superscripts (1), (2) and (3). Left: two segments of length one bend through (0,0), (0.8,0.6) and (1.6,0), so the endpoints are 1.6 apart. Right: straightened, the three points lie at 0, 1 and 2 on a line, the largest possible separation. RDM entries D12=1, D23=1 and D13=3 therefore cannot all be Euclidean distances, in any number of dimensions.
cosine_indexed.svg: Three unit image-response vectors: x^(1)=(1,0), x^(2)=(1/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)) and x^(3)=(0,1), at 0, 45 and 90 degrees. The cosine dissimilarity between the outer two is one, while the two adjacent pairs sum to 2−sqrt(2), about 0.586, which violates the triangle inequality.
directional_similarity.svg: Left: a map highlighting China in blue and North Korea in magenta, with a leader line to the much smaller North Korean outline. Right: two diagrams summarizing Tversky (1977). North Korea compared to China is judged more similar; China compared to North Korea is judged less similar. Reversing subject and referent changes the similarity judgment, whereas Euclidean distance is symmetric.
same_accuracy.svg: Ten wolf and husky photographs in two rows of five. Each card gives the true label and the predictions of classifiers A and B, marked correct or incorrect. Both classify seven of ten correctly, but their errors differ: A errs on images 1, 2 and 4, all wolves in snow; B errs on image 5, a wolf in grass, and images 6 and 7, huskies in snow. B follows a background rule: snow means wolf, no snow means husky. Photo credits are linked on the slide.
rgb_live.png: Left: the 224 by 224 color tiger photograph. Middle: its red, green and blue channels, labelled 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 values. Right: the three channel values of a selected pixel, the same values divided by 255, a color swatch and one bar per channel.
gray_live.png: Left: the 224 by 224 color tiger photograph, with the 8 by 8 region behind the selected pixel highlighted. Middle: the 28 by 28 grayscale intensity array, labelled 784 values. Right: the vector bold x, listed as its first four entries, 18, 27, 26 and 18, followed by an ellipsis, with the selected entry and its Python index.
bars_live.png: Left: the color tiger photograph. Middle: the 28 by 28 grayscale array. Right: all 784 grayscale values plotted in row order, with the selected entry highlighted in magenta. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 255; the horizontal axis is the position in the vector, not time.
tiger_relu.svg: The late ResNet-18 responses to the tiger photograph: all 4,096 stored activations in stored order, drawn as blue stems. Green marks below the baseline flag the exact zeros: 1,843 of them, or 45.0 percent; the maximum is 13.57. A small inset plots the ReLU: output a_j is zero for nonpositive input z_j and equal to the input for positive values.
